stem: A 16-year-old girl with known rheumatic heart disease, followed intermittently at a local clinic, presents with about six weeks of right-sided chest pain and progressive breathlessness, initially attributed by her family to her heart condition acting up. She has had low-grade fevers she hadn't mentioned because she assumed they were part of her usual health issues. No prior TB treatment, no known TB contact, no known drug-resistant contact. Chest exam and imaging reveal a moderate right-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis was performed; pleural fluid was sent for molecular testing (in addition to biochemical and ADA testing), which returned positive for M. tuberculosis. Exam: decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the right base, a known systolic murmur consistent with her rheumatic heart disease, no lower extremity edema.

patient.social_history: Lives with family in a rural household; known rheumatic heart disease followed intermittently
patient.presenting_complaint: Right-sided chest pain and progressive breathlessness, initially attributed to known heart disease
patient.exam_findings: Decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion at right base, known systolic murmur, no lower extremity edema, moderate right pleural effusion on imaging
patient.prior_treatment: None for this episode; no prior TB treatment ever

distractors: Worsening rheumatic heart disease proposed as sufficient explanation for the breathlessness and chest pain without considering a new, separate process
Low-grade fevers dismissed as an ordinary feature of her chronic condition rather than investigated as a new finding
A parapneumonic effusion from an unrecognized bacterial pneumonia proposed as an alternative cause of the pleural fluid
ntep_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the pleural fluid), alongside biochemical/ADA testing, as a first-line microbiological tool rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology alone.
who_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the pleural fluid), alongside biochemical/ADA testing, as a first-line microbiological tool rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology alone.
us_correct_actions: Anchor the diagnostic workup for this extrapulmonary presentation around culture and histology as the reference standard, treating molecular testing as a general, conditional adjunct rather than the upfront first-line tool for extrapulmonary specimens.
critical_error_conditions: Attributing the pleural effusion entirely to her known rheumatic heart disease and deferring pleural fluid sampling and molecular testing
expected_divergence_points: Whether upfront molecular testing on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen is the first-line diagnostic tool or culture/histology remains the anchoring reference standard
